Three request handlers, two stop callers, at most three accepted normal-priority items, one drain owner, one repeat task and at most one storage startup failure. Marker checks, startup settlement and queue retirement are separate actions.

A failed startup clears both cached owners. Only a later accepted request triggers another start; no autonomous retry is assumed or claimed. RetryRestoresDrain applies only after that later request actually starts the retry.

Fairness assumes enabled marker checks and storage-start attempts settle, a second storage attempt succeeds after the one allowed failure, the existing scheduler serves ready drain work, and disposal completes. Without that fairness, RetryWithoutFairness must produce a loop counterexample.

Stop retires admission before awaiting startup and repeated stop joins the existing cleanup. Successful disposal is assumed for StopSettles; failed cleanup, partial high-priority flush and failed durable task-row deletion are outside this projection. Already-accepted normal-priority work may be explicitly discarded during fast shutdown. Processing represents a terminal queue outcome, not proof of correct PII redaction, model completion, high-priority flush behavior or unbounded queue progress. The real PGlite hook checks task startup failure/retry and stop ownership; it does not enumerate every model schedule.

One original service, one sequential replacement, two rooms and four calls. Original room 0 has one optional cold reader or writer and a second writer. Original room 1 has one writer, and the replacement writes room 0.

Labels are distinct and below LRU capacity. Successful persistence replaces durable topics with the current local list. A failed write leaves local topics, so a later successful call can persist them. Failed hydration leaves the room cold.
The runtime suite uses real SQLite for plugin unload/reload, durable readback, persistence failure and recovery. Controlled I/O ports cover same-room ordering, independent rooms and pending stop.

Metadata mutations by unrelated writers, missing-room races, process crashes, unknown commits, duplicate labels, capacity eviction and simultaneous independent runtimes remain outside this finite projection.
